items.summary: BioCoder Python subset (157 instances): two prompting baselines and OpenHands CodeActAgent v1.5, 0-shot.
Gorilla APIBench (1775 instances): three prompted foundation-model baselines, a model fine-tuned specifically for API calls, and OpenHands CodeActAgent v1.5, 0-shot.
ToolQA, easy subset (800 instances): three non-agentic baselines, a ReAct 0-shot baseline at two model sizes, and OpenHands CodeActAgent v1.5, 0-shot.

OpenHands CodeActAgent v1.5 with gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 scored 2.3% on ToolQA (easy subset), far below the ReAct 0-shot baseline using a comparable-tier backbone (gpt-3.5-turbo, 36.8%), and below every other listed baseline on this benchmark.

WebArena (812 instances): four specialized/trained web-agent baselines, a zero-shot WebArena Agent baseline at two model sizes, and two OpenHands agents (BrowsingAgent v1.0; CodeActAgent v1.8 delegating to BrowsingAgent v1.0) each at three backbone LLMs.
MiniWoB++ (125 environments): two specialist trained-model baselines and two OpenHands agents.
On MiniWoB++, the best OpenHands configuration (BrowsingAgent v1.0 with gpt-4o, 40.8%) trails the specialist reinforcement-learning baseline CC-NET (91.1%) by a wide margin.
GAIA, L1 validation set (53 instances): AutoGPT baseline and OpenHands GPTSwarm v1.0 at two model versions.
GPQA diamond set (198 instances): expert and non-expert human baselines, two few-shot chain-of-thought LLM baselines, and OpenHands CodeActAgent v1.8.
AgentBench, OS (bash) subset (144 instances): AgentBench baseline agent at two model sizes and OpenHands CodeActAgent v1.5 at two model sizes.
MINT, math subset (225 instances): MINT baseline agent and OpenHands CodeActAgent v1.5 at two model sizes.
MINT, code subset (136 instances): MINT baseline agent and OpenHands CodeActAgent v1.5 at two model sizes.
On the MINT code subset, OpenHands' best configuration (gpt-4o, 50.0%) scored below the MINT Baseline Agent (gpt-4-0613, 59.6%).
ProofWriter, 5-hop subset (600 instances): a few-shot chain-of-thought baseline, a symbolic-solver-augmented baseline (Logic-LM), and OpenHands CodeActAgent v1.5.
Entity Deduction Arena (200 instances, average of two 100-instance sub-datasets): a zero-shot-prompting baseline at two model sizes and OpenHands CodeActAgent v1.5 at two model sizes.
On Entity Deduction Arena, OpenHands' best configuration (gpt-4o, 38.0%) scored below the zero-shot-prompting gpt-4-0314 baseline (40.0%).

Across Tables 4-6, every non-OpenHands comparison agent (SWE-Agent, AutoCodeRover, Aider, Moatless Tools, Agentless, Lemur, Patel et al., AutoWebGLM, Auto Eval & Refine, WebArena Agent, Workflow Guided Exploration, CC-NET, AutoGPT, AgentBench Baseline Agent, MINT Baseline Agent, Logic-LM, Gorilla-finetuned, ReAct, few-shot CoT/zero-shot prompting baselines) is reported in exactly one benchmark category (software, web, or miscellaneous), whereas the same OpenHands CodeActAgent (and, for web, BrowsingAgent) system prompt is evaluated across all three categories.
items.notes: This structural fact is directly countable from the tables; it is also asserted qualitatively by the authors themselves (see E025).

items.summary: Author-stated framing of the headline result: OpenHands agents may not top every category, but the same CodeAct agent, with no change to its system prompt, is competitive across software development, web interaction, and miscellaneous tasks -- which the authors call 'particularly significant' next to baseline agents that are each designed and optimized for one task category.
items.notes: Recorded as 'soft' because it is the authors' own prose interpretation, not a machine-produced number; it is nonetheless author_stated and central to the paper's contribution.

items.summary: OpenHands' agent state is a data structure whose central component is the event stream, a chronological record of past actions and observations (including user messages); the state also carries auxiliary bookkeeping (accumulated LLM cost, multi-agent delegation metadata, other execution parameters).

The core action types are IPythonRunCellAction and CmdRunAction (execute Python/bash inside the sandbox) and BrowserInteractiveAction (browser actions via a domain-specific language introduced by BrowserGym). The action space is described as inspired by CodeAct (Wang et al., 2024a) and as compatible with predefined-tool-calling agents, since tools can be defined as ordinary functions in the same programming languages.

For each task session OpenHands starts an isolated Docker container; inside it, an OpenHands-maintained 'action execution API' server exposes a bash shell, a Jupyter IPython server, and a Playwright-based Chromium browser (using BrowserGym action primitives: navigation, clicking, typing, scrolling); browser observations include HTML, DOM, accessibility tree, screenshot, and open tabs. A configurable workspace directory is mounted into the sandbox.

OpenHands supports arbitrary user-provided base Docker images: a build mechanism installs the action execution API into that image so agents can run inside any software environment the user specifies.

items.summary: AgentSkills is a Python package of utility functions auto-imported into the IPython environment, forming the agent-computer interface (ACI). A new skill is added only if (1) it is not readily achievable by having the LLM write code directly, or (2) it requires calling an external model. Listed skills include file-editing utilities adapted from SWE-Agent and Aider (edit_file, scroll_up/scroll_down, open_file, goto_line, create_file, search_dir/search_file/find_file) and multi-modal document parsers (parse_image, parse_pdf, parse_docx, parse_latex, parse_audio, parse_video, parse_pptx).

Agents can delegate a subtask to another agent via AgentDelegateAction; e.g. the generalist CodeActAgent, which has limited native browsing support, delegates web-browsing subtasks to the specialized BrowsingAgent.

AgentHub is described as containing more than 10 community-contributed agent implementations, including: CodeAct Agent (default generalist, based on the CodeAct framework, able to converse or act via bash/Python/browser code); Browsing Agent (a zero-shot generalist web baseline similar to the WebArena agent but with improved observations/actions); GPTSwarm Agent (uses optimizable graphs, Zhuge et al., 2024); and Micro Agents (task-specialized agents that reuse a generalist implementation and lower the barrier to sharing specialized prompts).

The evaluation framework integrates 15 benchmarks across three categories (software engineering: SWE-Bench, HumanEvalFix, BIRD, BioCoder, ML-Bench, Gorilla APIBench, ToolQA; web: WebArena, MiniWoB++; miscellaneous assistance: GAIA, GPQA, AgentBench, MINT, Entity Deduction Arena, ProofWriter), each mapped to a required agent capability.
OpenHands is released under the MIT license (permitting commercial use); as of writing it had 32K GitHub stars and more than 2.1K contributions ('PRs') from over 188 contributors.

OpenHands includes an end-to-end integration-test framework for agent quality control: developers define a task and an expected 'gold file'; the framework mocks LLM calls with stored prompt-response pairs (keyed by exact prompt match) for deterministic, low-cost regression testing, regenerating pairs only when prompts change substantially; tests run on every pull request and commit across multiple platforms and sandbox types.

Author-identified future-work directions: enhanced multi-modality (viewing images/video and processing spreadsheet files through the browser/IPython path); stronger agents via training and inference-time techniques (current agents 'still struggle with complex tasks'); better long-file editing (agents 'suffer a lot' editing long files); web-browsing improvements (planned integration of Auto Eval & Refine's Reflexion-based retry strategy); automatic workflow generation (graph-based frameworks such as GPTSwarm or LangGraph as candidate directions, since the current workflow 'still requires a substantial handcrafted workload').

The authors attribute part of the HumanEvalFix gap to protocol, not only capability: SWE-Agent's 87.7% used a 1-shot prompt containing a full demonstration trajectory of a successful fix on one of the test bugs, whereas OpenHands was evaluated 0-shot; the authors also state that, because HumanEvalFix bugs are human-created and validated, 100% is 'entirely feasible' and is a goal for future iterations.

Evaluation-protocol choices stated by the authors that limit direct comparability across rows of the same table: SWE-Bench is reported without the benchmark's optional 'hint text' throughout; SWE-Bench Lite (not the full 2294-instance set) is used 'for cost-saving consideration'; ML-Bench uses 'the quarter subset' (following the original paper's own setup); ToolQA uses 'the easy subset'; GPQA's headline number uses the 'diamond' set (full/extended-set results were attempted in Appendix G but that table's alignment did not survive extraction, E044). Baseline numbers throughout Tables 4-6 are drawn from the cited original papers rather than re-run by the authors under identical conditions.

The ethics statement is descriptive, not empirical: it asserts that most AI agents today 'lack the ability to perform complex, long-horizon tasks in the real world reliably', that improving agents pose 'security risks to society', and that OpenHands helps mitigate this via (1) enabling systematic evaluation, (2) facilitating human-agent interaction rather than fully autonomous operation, and (3) broadening researcher access to agent suites for safety research -- none of which is measured by a safety benchmark among the 15 evaluated.

A later, separate repository ('OpenHands Benchmarks') describes migrating evaluation infrastructure from what it calls 'OpenHands V0' to a new 'OpenHands Software Agent SDK' ('V1'), and lists currently active benchmarks -- SWE-Bench, SWE-Bench Pro, GAIA, Commit0, OpenAgentSafety, and ProgramBench -- none of the last three of which appear among the 15 benchmarks paper.txt reports. OpenAgentSafety is described as 'AI agent safety evaluation in workplace scenarios with NPC interactions'.

A later, separate repository README describes 'Agent Canvas', 'the self-hosted developer control center for coding agents and automations', which runs OpenHands or third-party agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, or any Agent-Client-Protocol-compatible agent) across local, remote, or cloud backends, with an optional commercial 'OpenHands Cloud'/'OpenHands Enterprise' offering, and a multi-repository architecture (OpenHands/OpenHands frontend; software-agent-sdk; typescript-client; automation).

A concrete, dated example of continued architectural change: SDK commit 79868ae5 (dated November 17, 2025) introduced a new 'openhands.sdk.critic' module that later benchmark code depends on, illustrating that the codebase evaluated in paper.txt (versions v1.5-v1.8, evaluated circa mid-to-late 2024) is a much earlier snapshot than the system described in the current READMEs.

items.summary: OpenHands (f.k.a. OpenDevin) was initially inspired by the AI software engineer Devin (Cognition.ai) but is stated to have since evolved to support a much wider range of applications through community contributions.

Related-work characterizations, in the authors' own words, of specific prior systems that motivate OpenHands' design: SWE-Agent 'highlights the importance of a carefully crafted Agent-Computer Interface ... in successfully solving complex tasks'; AutoGen 'advances beyond basic frameworks by implementing Python and bash execution capabilities, though with stateless command execution'; CrewAI offers 'sandboxed but limited code interpreter features'; LangChain/LangGraph 'provide foundational building blocks with basic runtime support'.
